note: Shot-size recommendations written by this app from general load-selection practice. NOT regulations, NOT CDFW content, NOT sourced to any official publication. Every band here is the app's own judgment and is deliberately uncited — the missing citation field is the honest signal, exactly as it is in equipment_guidance and in the angling tips. No record may state, imply or summarise a rule about gauge, shot size, shot material or method. What the regulations say is quoted, cited and free in hunt_methods.json; every record here links the records that bound it; and the build refuses any band that falls outside the ceiling those linked records state, so the advice cannot drift outside the law even by accident.

tips_disclaimer.headline: Shot-size notes — not regulations, not CDFW content
tips_disclaimer.body: Written by this app from general hunting practice. Nothing here is a rule and nothing here is permission. What the regulations say about gauge, shot size, shot material and method is quoted above with its citation. A recommendation on this card never widens what is quoted there, and where the two look different, the quoted rule is the one that counts.
tips_disclaimer.no_citation_line: No citation — this is not sourced to any regulation.

chip_definitions.nonlead: A statement about the pellet, not about the reader. Steel, bismuth and the tungsten alloys contain no lead; lead shot does. The statewide ammunition record is linked on every card in this file — read it there, in its own words.
chip_definitions.nontoxic_waterfowl: The same kind of statement, carried by the birds that have a materials record of their own. Ducks, geese, brant, coot and moorhen cards carry this chip, and the record that names the materials is linked on each of them.

quarry_size_definitions.small_bird: Under about half a pound, taken close and taken fast. Pattern density decides the outcome and pellet weight is barely in the argument.
quarry_size_definitions.medium_bird: Roughly half a pound to three pounds. Heavy enough that pellet weight starts to matter as much as pellet count, and the right answer moves with the range.
quarry_size_definitions.large_bird: Three pounds and up, with feather and bone in front of the vitals. Penetration is the problem, and the coarse end of the band is the working answer rather than the exception.
quarry_size_definitions.small_mammal: Rabbits, hares and tree squirrels. Thin-skinned but densely furred, and almost always shot through cover or at an upward angle that has already thinned the pattern.

shot_sizes.distance_framing: Inside 30 yards — birds crossing a watered field or funnelling through a gap — No. 7½ puts the most pellets into a small target. From 30 to 40 yards, and on late-season birds riding a wind, No. 6 still carries the energy that 7½ has started to give up. Density is what kills a dove; pellet weight is what reaches it.

records.reason: Small, thin-skinned and fast, taken at moderate range — a pattern-density problem rather than a penetration problem, and the fine half of the band is where most dove fields are won.
records.watch_out: Steel is less dense than lead, so a steel pellet of a given number arrives with less than the lead pellet of that number once did; the tungsten alloys go the other way and hit harder than their number suggests. Choose for the material in the shell, not for the number you grew up with.

shot_sizes.distance_framing: Roughly twice the body weight of a mourning dove and usually taken closer — around farmsteads, feed and water. No. 7½ is plenty inside 25 yards, but No. 6 is the better all-round choice, because these birds sit heavier and take a pellet better than their smaller cousins.

records.reason: The same shells as a dove field, one step coarser. The extra body weight is worth a slightly heavier pellet, and nothing about the shooting distance asks for more than that.
records.watch_out: These birds live where people do. Choose the shot for the bird and the direction of fire for everything behind it.

shot_sizes.distance_framing: A covey rise in cover is 15 to 25 yards and over in two seconds — No. 7½ and the most open choke you own. Late-season birds that run ahead of the dog and flush wild at 30 to 35 yards are the case for No. 6, and for a tighter choke before a coarser pellet.

records.reason: A quail is small and the shot is usually quick and close, so pattern width and pellet count beat pellet size nearly every time you go afield.
records.watch_out: Mountain quail in steep cover flush downhill and stretch out fast. That is the one quail situation where the coarse end of the band is a considered choice rather than an over-reaction.

shot_sizes.distance_framing: Chukar flush below you and go downhill fast, which turns a 25-yard bird into a 40-yard bird while you are still mounting the gun. No. 6 is the working answer for that. No. 7½ is for the covey that holds tight in front of a dog and gets up inside 25 yards.

records.reason: Tougher and more heavily feathered than a quail, and almost always shot going away and dropping — the extra pellet weight is what still gets through at the back end of the shot.
records.watch_out: The distance you think you shot at in chukar country is usually short of the truth. Pattern the gun at 40 yards before deciding the load is fine.

shot_sizes.distance_framing: Over a good dog inside 30 yards, No. 6 is enough bird-for-pellet. Wild late-season roosters getting up at 35 to 45 yards are what No. 5 and No. 4 are for — a rooster carries a lot of feather and a long tail that makes him look closer than he is.

records.reason: A big, heavily feathered bird that runs after it is hit. This is the first upland bird where penetration matters more than pattern density, which is why the band starts where the small-bird band ends.
records.watch_out: Cripples cost more birds than misses do on pheasant. If you are picking up runners, go one step coarser before you go one step tighter on choke.

shot_sizes.distance_framing: A turkey is killed in the head and neck, not the body, so this is a patterning problem measured on paper at the distance you actually intend to shoot — for most hunters 40 yards and in. No. 5 is the broad answer. No. 4 for the longest shot you would take; No. 6 when your gun and choke put enough pellets inside a ten-inch circle with it. The dense tungsten loads change the arithmetic completely and are commonly run finer still.

records.reason: The target is a few square inches of head and neck. How many pellets land inside that circle at your chosen distance decides the outcome; pellet size matters only because it changes how many of them arrive with enough left to break bone.
records.watch_out: Pattern the specific gun, choke and shell together on paper before the season opens. A turkey load that patterns beautifully in one barrel can leave holes in another, and no shot size fixes that.

shot_sizes.distance_framing: Forest grouse are close-cover birds — most shots are inside 25 yards through timber, where No. 7½ and the most open choke you own do the work. No. 6 is for the bird that flushes across an opening and is already 35 yards out before the gun is up.

records.reason: Not a hard bird to kill, but a hard bird to hit. Everything about the load should be aimed at a wide, even pattern arriving quickly.
records.watch_out: A sooty grouse sitting high in a conifer is a different shot from a ruffed grouse in an alder bottom. The vertical shot is longer than it looks and is the one worth carrying the coarser shell for.

shot_sizes.distance_framing: Band-tails are usually pass-shot high over a ridge, a mineral spring or a fruiting tree, and the birds are further out than the eye wants to believe. No. 6 for the ordinary pass at 30 to 40 yards; No. 7½ only for close birds decoying to water.

records.reason: A big, fast, high-flying pigeon shot at genuine distance. This is the bird on the upland page where hunters most often under-estimate the range and under-gun the shot as a result.
records.watch_out: The season is short and the bag is small, so every shell counts more than usual. Range estimation, not shot size, is what most band-tail hunters actually need to fix.

shot_sizes.distance_framing: Snipe get up underfoot and jink, so most shots are taken inside 25 yards, once the bird has settled into a line. No. 7½ throughout. No. 6 only if the same gun is carrying you through a duck marsh on the same morning.

records.reason: A very small bird, taken very close, on erratic flight. Pattern density and an open choke are the whole answer, and a coarser pellet only subtracts pellets from a pattern that needs every one of them.
records.watch_out: Snipe are hunted on wet ground where ducks are also flying. What suits one bird is not what suits the other, and swapping shells in a hurry is how the wrong shell gets fired.

shot_sizes.distance_framing: Teal, wood ducks and wigeon decoying inside 25 yards are a No. 4 proposition. Mallards and pintail working the blocks at 25 to 35 yards are what No. 2 and No. 3 are for. BB is for big late-season divers and for the pass shot at 40 yards and beyond, where the pellet has to still be carrying when it arrives.

records.reason: Steel and the other nontoxic materials give up speed and energy faster than lead did, so duck loads are chosen a size or two coarser than the lead numbers older references quote. The band is wide because a teal over decoys and a late-season diver on a pass are genuinely different problems.
records.watch_out: Going coarser than the shot needs empties the pattern. Most missed ducks are missed rather than under-penetrated, and a hole in the pattern at 35 yards is what a BB load buys you when the shot was really a 25-yard shot.

shot_sizes.distance_framing: Snow geese and specklebellies decoying inside 30 yards die cleanly to No. 2 and BB. Big Canada geese, and any goose at 40 yards and past it, are what BBB and T are for. Body weight and range move together here more than with any other bird on this list.

records.reason: A large bird with heavy feathers and a lot of bone in front of the vitals. Penetration is the whole problem, and the coarse end of the band exists because the pellet has to still be moving once it is through all of that.
records.watch_out: Coarse pellets mean few pellets. A T-shot load in a small gauge can put so few pellets in the air that a 30-yard goose flies through the pattern, which is why BB is the working answer over decoys rather than the biggest thing on the shelf.

shot_sizes.distance_framing: Brant are a coastal, close-decoying bird and a good deal smaller than a Canada goose — most shots are inside 30 yards over the eelgrass. No. 2 covers nearly all of it. No. 4 for birds in tight, and BB only for the long, windy edge of the day.

records.reason: Sized between a big duck and a small goose, and hunted at duck ranges. A goose load is more pellet than a brant needs and costs pattern for nothing.
records.watch_out: The temptation is to load for a goose because the bird is one. Brant are not Canadas, and the goose end of the shelf is the wrong end for them.

shot_sizes.distance_framing: Coot are usually taken close, on or just off the water, inside 30 yards. No. 6 is enough for that. No. 4 for birds getting up at the far edge of the decoys, or running along the surface before they lift.

records.reason: A soft-bodied bird taken at short range, but one that dives and swims off when hit lightly — which argues for a pellet with enough weight to finish the job rather than the finest thing in the bag.
records.watch_out: A lightly hit coot goes under and is rarely recovered. That, rather than the shot size, is the reason to pass on the long ones.

shot_sizes.distance_framing: A cottontail bolting through brush at 20 yards is a No. 7½ or No. 6 shot. A jackrabbit at 35 to 45 yards across open ground is a different animal entirely, and is what No. 4 is for — bigger body, tougher hide, longer shot.

records.reason: The band is wide because it covers two very different animals. Cottontails are small and close; jackrabbits are large and taken at distance, and one shell will not do both well.
records.watch_out: Brush eats pattern. Where the shot has to go through cover, an open choke and more pellets beat a coarser pellet and a tighter choke almost every time.

shot_sizes.distance_framing: The shot that matters is straight up into a canopy at 25 to 40 yards, through branches and leaves. No. 6 is the working answer. No. 4 is for the high, heavy-timber shot where the pellet has to arrive with something left after clipping a limb.

records.reason: A small animal with a surprisingly tough hide and dense fur, taken at an awkward upward angle where the pattern has already been thinned by cover. Pellet weight buys back the margin the angle takes away.
records.watch_out: Shooting up means everything that misses keeps going. Know what is beyond the tree, and treat a canopy as cover rather than as a backstop.

records.why: We publish no shot recommendation for greater sage-grouse. Read the seasons table above first — for this bird it decides whether there is a hunt at all in a given year, and in some years the answer is no. Beyond that, this is a hunt very few Californians ever go on, and we have no general practice worth passing on that would not simply be us guessing on your behalf.

species_join.value: Spotted Dove, and Ringed Turtle Dove

records.why: We publish no separate shot recommendation for spotted dove or ringed turtle dove. Both are on the table above because the regulations name them, but the birds themselves are scarce and scattered enough in California that almost nobody sets out for one on purpose. If you do take a shot at one it will be from a dove field, and the mourning dove card is the honest answer — we would rather send you there than invent a distinct recommendation for a bird we have no distinct practice for.
